newsitem.title: USA: OfficeMax resumes talks with Staples.
newsitem.headline: OfficeMax resumes talks with Staples.

text.p: OfficeMax resumed talks Tuesday to acquire dozens of stores from Staples Inc., in a last-ditch effort to satisfy government trustbusters who object to a $4 billion merger between Staples and rival office supply chain Office Depot.

Sources close to the talks said Staples was looking at new proposals from OfficeMax, only one day after the Federal Trade Commission voted 4-1 to go into federal court and seek an injunction to halt the proposed merger.
Although both the FTC and Staples have expressed confidence they can win in court, it is also possible a court fight could bog down and delay final completion of a merger for months or even years.
Now it appears OfficeMax -- the only office superstore chain in the United States in addition to Staples and Office Depot -- may hold the key to opening the way for a merger.

Federal Trade Commission officials were willing to approve a merger if Staples divested 62 stores to OfficeMax, those close to the talks say. They would not consider the sales of Staples stores to others, the sources say.
But negotiations between Staples and OfficeMax broke down over a dispute about which stores would change hands, with money also an issue.
OfficeMax accepted 52 of the stores proposed by Staples but wanted 20 others of its own choosing, sources said.
While Staples wanted $150 million to $160 million for the mix of 62 stores it was offering to sell, OfficeMax was willing to pay only $100 million for the more than 70 stores it wanted to buy.

All sides are now working against a major deadline, which has not yet been set: A court hearing to consider the FTC's bid for a permanent injunction against the merger. Such a hearing, before a U.S. District Court judge, is expected to begin in one to eight weeks.
A Staples official said any chance of a merger would be over if the government wins a preliminary injunction and sustains the win on appeal.
But even if Staples does not lose, it may find delays difficult to handle.

For example, a judge could permit the stores to merge but force them to hold their assets separate until a final resolution. Such a final resolution would first require the workings of FTC administrative law, which would take at least 13 months. With appeals, the process could take far longer.
